cards.q: What is a hydrocarbon?
cards.a: A compound of hydrogen and carbon only.
cards.why: Ethanol, \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}OH}\), contains carbon and hydrogen but is not a hydrocarbon: it also contains oxygen.

cards.q: What is a homologous series?
cards.a: A series of compounds with the same functional group and the same general formula, in which each member differs from the next by \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\).
cards.why: Members have similar chemical properties and show a gradual trend in physical properties such as boiling point.

cards.q: What is a functional group?
cards.a: An atom or group of atoms that is responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions of a molecule.
cards.why: For example, \(\mathrm{-OH}\) in alcohols and \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) in alkenes.

cards.q: Define empirical formula and molecular formula.
cards.a:
Empirical formula: the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
Molecular formula: the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule.
cards.why: Hexane: molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{14}}\), empirical formula \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{7}}\).

cards.q: Give the general formulae of the alkanes, the alkenes and the alcohols.
cards.a: Alkanes \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+2}}\); alkenes \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}\); alcohols \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n+1}OH}\).
cards.why: A general formula is the simplest algebraic formula for any member of a homologous series.

cards.q: What is the difference between a structural, a displayed and a skeletal formula?
cards.a:
Structural: the minimal arrangement of atoms, e.g. \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}}\).
Displayed: every atom and every bond drawn.
Skeletal: carbon chain as zig-zag lines, with C atoms and the H atoms on them left out; functional groups shown.
cards.why: In a skeletal formula every line end and every corner is a carbon atom.

cards.q: Draw the displayed formula of propan-2-ol, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}}\).
cards.a: Every bond is shown, including the O–H bond.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of propan-2-ol: three carbons in a row, every C–H bond drawn, with an O–H group on the middle carbon.

cards.why: A common slip is writing –OH without the O–H bond: in a displayed formula every bond must be drawn.

cards.q: Draw the displayed formula of ethanoic acid, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}\).
cards.a: The carboxyl carbon has a C=O double bond and a C–O single bond to the O–H group.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed formula of ethanoic acid: a CH3 carbon with three C–H bonds joined to a carbon that has a C=O double bond and a single bond to an O–H group.

cards.why: The acid in vinegar. The carboxyl group contains two different C–O bonds, so both must be drawn.

cards.q: Give the molecular formula and the empirical formula of the compound shown.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 3-methylbutan-1-ol: a four-carbon chain ending in OH, with a methyl branch on the third carbon from the OH.

cards.a: Molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}O}\); empirical formula also \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}O}\).
steps: Count the carbons: every line end and corner is a carbon, giving 5.
Each carbon has 4 bonds: add hydrogens to make up 4. \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) ×2, \(\mathrm{CH}\) ×1, \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\) ×2, plus the H of OH: \(6 + 1 + 4 + 1 = 12\).
The ratio 5 : 12 : 1 cannot be simplified, so the empirical formula is the same.
cards.why: Forgetting the hydrogen on the oxygen is the most common counting error.

cards.q: Give the empirical formula of butane, \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{10}}\), and of cyclohexane, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}}\).
cards.a: Butane \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{5}}\); cyclohexane \(\mathrm{CH_{2}}\).
cards.why: Every alkene and cycloalkane has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>, so it cannot tell them apart.

cards.q: Give the stem for chains of 1 to 10 carbon atoms.
cards.a: 1 meth, 2 eth, 3 prop, 4 but, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 hept, 8 oct, 9 non, 10 dec.
cards.why: The stem names the longest carbon chain that contains the functional group.

cards.q: Give the suffix or prefix used in IUPAC names for: alkene, alcohol, aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, halogenoalkane.
cards.a: -ene; -ol; -al; -one; -oic acid; prefix chloro-, bromo- or iodo-.
cards.why: Halogens and alkyl branches are prefixes; the main functional group gives the suffix.

cards.q: Name this branched alkane.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a five-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the second carbon.

cards.a: 2-methylpentane
cards.why: Longest chain 5 (pent-); number from the end nearer the branch, so the methyl is on C2, not C4.

cards.q: Name this alkane, which has two branches on one carbon.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain with two methyl groups on the second carbon.

cards.a: 2,2-dimethylbutane
cards.why: Two identical groups take "di", and a locant is given for each, even when they are on the same carbon.

cards.q: Name this halogenoalkane.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain with Br on the second carbon and a methyl group on the third.

cards.a: 2-bromo-3-methylbutane
cards.why: Numbering from either end gives locants 2 and 3, so the tie goes to the prefix first in the alphabet: bromo before methyl.

cards.q: Name this alcohol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain with OH on the second carbon.

cards.a: butan-2-ol
cards.why: Number from the end that gives the –OH the lowest locant: 2, not 3.

cards.q: Name this aldehyde.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a four-carbon chain ending in a C=O group at the end of the chain (an aldehyde group).

cards.a: butanal
cards.why: The aldehyde carbon is always C1 and is counted in the chain, so no number is needed.

cards.q: Name this ketone, which has the same number of carbons on each side of the C=O.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a five-carbon chain with C=O on the middle carbon.

cards.a: pentan-3-one
cards.why: From five carbons upwards a ketone needs a locant: pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one are different compounds.

cards.q: Name this carboxylic acid.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a carboxylic acid: a COOH carbon joined to a carbon that carries a methyl branch and a methyl end.

cards.a: 2-methylpropanoic acid
cards.why: The COOH carbon is C1 and is counted in the chain: three carbons (propanoic acid) with a methyl on C2.

cards.q: Name this compound, used in cosmetics and soaps.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a three-carbon chain with an OH group on every carbon.

cards.a: propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol)
cards.why: With "di" or "tri" before -ol, the "e" of the stem is kept: propane-, not propan-.

cards.q: Name this cyclic hydrocarbon.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a six-membered carbon ring containing one double bond.

cards.a: cyclohexene
cards.why: Cyclohexane, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}}\), is saturated; cyclohexene, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{10}}\), has one C=C.

cards.q: Name this ketone.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a five-carbon chain with C=O on the second carbon and a methyl branch on the fourth.

cards.a: 4-methylpentan-2-one
cards.why: The functional group (C=O) gets the lowest number, then the branch is numbered from that end.

cards.q: Draw the skeletal formula of 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
cards.a: A central carbon bonded to an OH group and to three methyl groups.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-methylpropan-2-ol: a central carbon with three methyl lines and an OH.

cards.why: Its structural formula is \(\mathrm{(CH_{3})_{3}COH}\): a tertiary alcohol.

cards.q: Draw the skeletal formula of 3-methylbut-1-ene.
cards.a: A four-carbon chain with the C=C between C1 and C2, and a methyl group on C3.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 3-methylbut-1-ene: a terminal C=C double bond, then a carbon carrying two methyl groups.

cards.why: Structural formula \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CHCH(CH_{3})_{2}}\).

cards.q: Draw the skeletal formula of 1,2-dichloropropane.
cards.a: A three-carbon chain with a Cl on C1 and a Cl on C2.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of 1,2-dichloropropane: a three-carbon chain with chlorine on the first and second carbons.

cards.why: Structural formula \(\mathrm{CH_{2}ClCHClCH_{3}}\).

cards.q: A student names this compound "2-ethylbutane". What is wrong, and what is its correct name?

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of a five-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the middle carbon, drawn so that it could be misread as a butane chain with an ethyl branch.

cards.a: The longest chain was not chosen. The correct name is 3-methylpentane.
cards.why: An ethyl group on C2 always lengthens the main chain; trace every path through the molecule to find the longest one.

cards.q: True or false: "1-methylpropane" is a correct IUPAC name.
cards.a: False. A methyl on the end carbon just extends the chain: the compound is butane.
cards.why: A branch can never be on C1 of an alkyl chain: that carbon is part of the longest chain.

cards.q: When a molecule has several different substituents, in what order are the prefixes written?
cards.a: In alphabetical order, ignoring multiplying prefixes such as di- and tri-.
cards.why: So 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylpentane: "chloro" comes before "methyl", and the "di" is ignored.

cards.q: Classify this reaction of ethene.

figure.alt: Ethene reacts with bromine to give 1,2-dibromoethane.

cards.a: Addition
cards.why: Two molecules combine to form one product; the C=C becomes a C–C single bond.

cards.q: Classify this reaction of ethanol.

figure.alt: Ethanol is heated with concentrated phosphoric acid to give ethene and water.

cards.a: Elimination (dehydration)
cards.why: A small molecule (water) is removed from adjacent carbons, forming a C=C double bond.

cards.q: Classify this reaction of propan-2-ol.

figure.alt: Propan-2-ol is heated with acidified potassium dichromate to give propanone.

cards.a: Oxidation
cards.why: The alcohol loses hydrogen: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3} + [O] \rightarrow CH_{3}COCH_{3} + H_{2}O}\).

cards.q: Classify this reaction of propanone.

figure.alt: Propanone reacts with lithium tetrahydridoaluminate in dry ether to give propan-2-ol.

cards.a: Reduction
cards.why: The ketone gains hydrogen: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}COCH_{3} + 2[H] \rightarrow CH_{3}CH(OH)CH_{3}}\).

cards.q: Classify this reaction in two ways.

figure.alt: Bromoethane reacts with hydroxide ions to give ethanol and bromide ions.

cards.a: Substitution, and also hydrolysis.
cards.why: An –OH replaces the –Br (substitution), and the C–Br bond is broken by reaction with water or hydroxide ions (hydrolysis).

cards.q: What is meant by hydrolysis, and by polymerisation?
cards.a:
Hydrolysis: splitting a bond by reaction with water.
Polymerisation: joining many small molecules (monomers) into a long chain (a polymer).
cards.why: Hydrolysis of an ester gives a carboxylic acid and an alcohol; ethene polymerises to poly(ethene).

cards.q: What does a curly arrow represent in a reaction mechanism?
cards.a: The movement of a pair of electrons.
cards.why: A fish-hook (half-headed) arrow shows the movement of a single electron.

cards.q: Where must a curly arrow start, and where does it end?
cards.a: It starts from a lone pair or from a covalent bond. It ends at an atom, or between two atoms where a new bond forms.
cards.why: An arrow starting at an atom or a charge, rather than at a lone pair or bond, loses the mark.

cards.q: In this step, identify the nucleophile and say what each curly arrow shows.

figure.alt: Nucleophilic substitution: a lone pair on the hydroxide ion attacks the δ+ carbon of bromoethane, and the C–Br bond breaks to give a bromide ion.

cards.a: Nucleophile: \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\). Arrow 1: a lone pair on O forms a new bond to the \(\delta+\) carbon. Arrow 2: the C–Br bond breaks, both electrons going to Br.
cards.why: Bond forming and bond breaking each need their own arrow.

cards.q: Define nucleophile and electrophile.
cards.a:
Nucleophile: an electron pair donor.
Electrophile: an electron pair acceptor.
cards.why: Nucleophiles (\(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{CN^{-}}\), \(\mathrm{NH_{3}}\)) have a lone pair; electrophiles (\(\mathrm{H^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{NO_{2}^{+}}\)) are attracted to electron-rich regions.

cards.q: What is heterolytic fission? Describe what happens in this step.

figure.alt: Heterolytic fission: in 2-bromo-2-methylpropane the δ+ carbon is bonded to a δ− bromine; a curly arrow from the C–Br bond to Br shows both electrons going to bromine, giving a tertiary carbocation and a bromide ion.

cards.a: Heterolytic fission: a covalent bond breaks so that both electrons go to one atom, forming two ions. Here both C–Br electrons go to the more electronegative Br, giving a carbocation and a bromide ion.
cards.why: Compare homolytic fission, in which each atom keeps one electron and two radicals form.

cards.q: What is a radical, and how is it shown in a mechanism?
cards.a: A species with an unpaired electron, shown by a dot, e.g. \(\mathrm{Cl\bullet}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_{3}\bullet}\).
cards.why: Curly arrows are not required for radical mechanisms: write balanced equations for each step instead.

cards.q: Describe what each of the three curly arrows shows in this mechanism.

figure.alt: Electrophilic addition: the C=C double bond of ethene attacks the δ+ hydrogen of HBr, the H–Br bond breaks, and the bromide ion then attacks the carbocation.

cards.a: 1: the C=C electron pair forms a bond to the \(\delta+\) H. 2: the H–Br bond breaks, both electrons going to Br. 3: a lone pair on \(\mathrm{Br^{-}}\) forms a bond to the carbocation.
cards.why: Every new bond in a mechanism comes from an electron pair, either a lone pair or a bond.

cards.q: True or false: a curly arrow from the negative charge of \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) to a carbon atom is correct.
cards.a: False. The arrow must start from a lone pair on the oxygen atom, drawn as two dots.
cards.why: The charge is not an electron pair. Examiners want the lone pair drawn and the arrow starting from it.

cards.q: Define structural isomers.
cards.a: Compounds with the same molecular formula but a different structural formula.
cards.why: The three types are chain, position and functional group isomers.

cards.q: Draw the three structural isomers of \(\mathrm{C_{5}H_{12}}\) and name them.
cards.a: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of the three isomers of C5H12: pentane, a five-carbon zig-zag; 2-methylbutane, a four-carbon zig-zag with a branch on the second carbon; 2,2-dimethylpropane, one carbon joined to four others.

cards.why: These are chain isomers: same functional group, different carbon skeleton.

cards.q: How many structural isomers does \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{14}}\) have? Name them.
cards.a: Five: hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane, 2,3-dimethylbutane.
cards.why: Check for duplicates: "4-methylpentane" is 2-methylpentane numbered from the wrong end.

cards.q: Draw and name the four structural isomers of \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{9}Br}\).
cards.a: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of the four isomers of C4H9Br: 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane (top row), 1-bromo-2-methylpropane and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (bottom row).

cards.why: Two chains (butane, methylpropane), each with Br in two different positions.

cards.q: Draw the four structural isomers of \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}Cl_{2}}\).
cards.a: 1,1-dichloropropane, 1,2-dichloropropane, 1,3-dichloropropane and 2,2-dichloropropane.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of the four isomers of C3H6Cl2: 1,1-, 1,2-, 1,3- and 2,2-dichloropropane.

cards.why: These are position isomers: the carbon chain is the same; only the positions of the chlorines differ.

cards.q: Propanal and propanone are both \(\mathrm{C_{3}H_{6}O}\). What type of isomers are they?

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of propanal, a three-carbon chain ending in an aldehyde group, and propanone, with C=O on the middle carbon.

cards.a: Functional group isomers: an aldehyde and a ketone.
cards.why: Same molecular formula, different functional groups, so different chemical properties.

cards.q: Give a functional group isomer of hex-1-ene, \(\mathrm{C_{6}H_{12}}\).
cards.a: Cyclohexane (or any cycloalkane, such as methylcyclopentane).

answerFigure.alt: Hex-1-ene, a six-carbon chain with a terminal double bond, and cyclohexane, a six-membered ring.

cards.why: Alkenes and cycloalkanes share the general formula \(\mathrm{C_{n}H_{2n}}\).

cards.q: Ethanol and methoxymethane are both \(\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}O}\). Why does ethanol boil at 78 °C but methoxymethane at −24 °C?

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of ethanol, a two-carbon chain ending in OH, and methoxymethane, an oxygen joining two methyl groups.

cards.a: They are functional group isomers. Ethanol has an \(\mathrm{O{-}H}\) group so it forms hydrogen bonds between molecules; methoxymethane has no O–H and cannot.
cards.why: Isomers with different functional groups can have very different physical as well as chemical properties.

cards.q: Identify the type of isomerism shown by each pair: (a) butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol; (b) butane and methylpropane; (c) propanoic acid and methyl ethanoate.
cards.a: (a) position; (b) chain; (c) functional group.
cards.why: Ask: is the functional group the same? If so, is the skeleton the same (position) or different (chain)?

cards.q: Define stereoisomers.
cards.a: Compounds with the same structural formula but a different arrangement of the atoms in space.
cards.why: E/Z isomerism is one kind of stereoisomerism; optical isomerism is another.

cards.q: Explain why E/Z isomerism can occur in alkenes.
cards.a: Restricted rotation about the planar C=C double bond, with two different groups on each carbon.
marks: There is restricted rotation about the C=C double bond.
The π bond would have to break for the groups to rotate.
Each carbon of the C=C must carry two different groups.

cards.q: Draw the E and Z isomers of but-2-ene.
cards.a: Z: both \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) groups on the same side. E: on opposite sides.

answerFigure.alt: Displayed C=C of the two isomers of but-2-ene. Z-but-2-ene: both CH3 groups on the top side of the double bond. E-but-2-ene: one CH3 on top of the left carbon, the other on the bottom of the right carbon.

cards.why: Z from German zusammen (together); E from entgegen (opposite). Z-but-2-ene is also called cis-but-2-ene.

cards.q: Is this the E or the Z isomer of 1,2-dichloroethene?

figure.alt: Displayed formula of 1,2-dichloroethene: one chlorine is on the top of the left carbon and the other on the bottom of the right carbon.

cards.a: E
cards.why: On each carbon Cl has the higher priority, and the two Cl atoms are on opposite sides of the double bond.

cards.q: How are the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) priority rules used to decide whether an isomer is E or Z?
cards.a: On each carbon of the C=C, the atom with the higher atomic number has higher priority. If the two higher-priority groups are on the same side, the isomer is Z; on opposite sides, E.
cards.why: If the atoms joined to the C=C are the same, compare the atoms attached to them, until there is a difference.

cards.q: Is this isomer of 3-chloropent-2-ene E or Z?

figure.alt: Displayed formula of 3-chloropent-2-ene: on the left carbon CH3 is on top and H below; on the right carbon CH2CH3 is on top and Cl below.

cards.a: E
cards.why: Left carbon: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) beats H. Right carbon: Cl (atomic number 17) beats \(\mathrm{CH_{2}CH_{3}}\) (C, 6), even though ethyl is bigger. \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) and Cl are on opposite sides.

cards.q: In this isomer of 2-bromobut-2-ene the two methyl groups are on opposite sides. True or false: it is the E isomer.

figure.alt: Displayed formula of 2-bromobut-2-ene: on the left carbon CH3 is on top and Br below; on the right carbon H is on top and CH3 below.

cards.a: False. It is the Z isomer.
cards.why: Left carbon: Br outranks \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\). Right carbon: \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) outranks H. Br and that \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\) are on the same side, so Z. E/Z is not always the same as trans/cis.

cards.q: Which of these shows E/Z isomerism: pent-1-ene, pent-2-ene, 2-methylbut-2-ene?

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of pent-1-ene (double bond at the end of a five-carbon chain), pent-2-ene (double bond between the second and third carbons) and 2-methylbut-2-ene (a four-carbon chain with the double bond between C2 and C3 and a methyl branch on C2).

cards.a: Only pent-2-ene.
cards.why: Pent-1-ene has two H atoms on C1; 2-methylbut-2-ene has two CH<sub>3</sub> groups on C2. Both double-bond carbons must have two different groups.

cards.q: Name this alkene, including its stereochemistry.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of pent-2-ene in which the chain continues on opposite sides of the double bond.

cards.a: (E)-pent-2-ene
cards.why: On each carbon of the C=C the alkyl group outranks H, and the two alkyl groups are on opposite sides.

cards.q: When can E/Z isomers also be named cis and trans?
cards.a: When two of the substituent groups on the C=C are the same (one on each carbon), as in but-2-ene.
cards.why: Cis: the identical groups on the same side; trans: on opposite sides. E/Z works for any substituents.

cards.q: How many isomers with a C=C, including stereoisomers, does \(\mathrm{C_{4}H_{8}}\) have? Name them.
cards.a: Four: but-1-ene, (E)-but-2-ene, (Z)-but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of the four alkenes C4H8: but-1-ene, (E)-but-2-ene with the chain ends on opposite sides of the double bond, (Z)-but-2-ene with both ends on the same side, and 2-methylpropene.

cards.why: Cyclobutane and methylcyclopropane are also C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, but have no C=C.

cards.q: True or false: Z- and E-but-2-ene can be converted into each other by rotating about the C=C bond at room temperature.
cards.a: False. They are separate compounds.
cards.why: Rotation would break the π bond, which needs far more energy than is available at room temperature.
